THOUGHT: The patient is a 40-year-old male with progressive, symmetric proximal muscle weakness (difficulty climbing stairs — lower limb proximal weakness; difficulty brushing hair — upper limb proximal weakness), over several months. Key clinical features include:  
- Proximal-predominant muscle weakness without sensory, cerebellar, or cranial nerve deficits (neuro exam otherwise normal), making primary neurogenic or peripheral neuropathic causes unlikely.  
- Muscle tenderness on palpation in shoulders and thighs — suggestive of active myofiber inflammation/injury.  
- Elevated creatine kinase (CK) and aldolase — classic biomarkers of skeletal muscle damage.  
- Normal ESR argues against systemic vasculitis or some chronic inflammatory conditions but does not exclude autoimmune myopathy (e.g., inclusion body myositis or immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy may have normal ESR).  
- Slightly elevated liver enzymes may reflect muscle origin (e.g., AST/ALT can rise with myolysis) or be incidental; however, in context of myositis, transaminitis is common and often disproportionate to hepatic involvement.  
- EMG shows myopathic changes — confirming primary muscle pathology.  
- Muscle biopsy reveals CD8+ lymphocyte infiltration in the endomysium — highly characteristic of T-cell–mediated autoimmune myopathy. This pattern (endomysial CD8+ T cells invading non-necrotic fibers) is the hallmark of polymyositis (PM). While dermatomyositis (DM) shows perivascular/perimysial inflammation and microangiopathy, and inclusion body myositis (IBM) shows rimmed vacuoles and intramuscular protein aggregates, the biopsy here specifically notes endomysial CD8+ infiltration — the defining histopathologic feature of polymyositis.  
- Absence of skin rash, dysphagia, interstitial lung disease, or Raynaud’s makes DM less likely. No rimmed vacuoles or filamentous inclusions are mentioned, making IBM less likely — and IBM typically has more insidious onset and poorer response to immunotherapy, but also commonly affects distal muscles and shows asymmetric involvement, which is not seen here.  
- Age (40 years), subacute progression, absence of malignancy red flags (though screening would still be prudent), and lack of other systemic symptoms further support idiopathic inflammatory myopathy — most specifically polymyositis.

DIAGNOSIS: Polymyositis
